title: German Cars Lost to Chinese EVs, and AfD's Rise Is Just a Symptom
dek: AfD is not a German problem but a Western one: people feel tomorrow won't be better, and Germany's proud cars, chemicals and railways all losing competitiveness at once is the real fuel for the far right.
why: The first half covers AfD and German social mood; the second half is the substance: the AI value chain, the 80/20 intelligence split, and what Europe lacks is someone who can make the call.
who: Investors watching European politics and industrial competitiveness, founders building for or expanding into Europe, and engineers who want to understand the geopolitics of the AI value chain.
skip: The opening linguistics discussion about German gender-inclusive language reform can be skipped; it has little bearing on the main argument.

points.h: AfD is not a German disease, it's a Western one
points.body: Judith Dada argues AfD's rise is not a German-only phenomenon: the US, France, the Netherlands and the UK all show the same tendency — people feel left behind, feel tomorrow won't be better than today or yesterday, and carry a melancholy for ‘the slower world of the past where their value in the environment was clearer’. She stresses at the same time that AfD is ‘the ugliest expression’ of this problem — among all far-right parties in Europe it is one of the most extreme, in some respects with regrettable similarities to Nazism. But she refuses to treat it as a fringe right-wing problem: in Saxony-Anhalt more than four in ten people voted for it, which shows the problem is societal and needs drastic political change, plus a vision of the future that can bring people along.

points.h: The neighbour who votes AfD is actually friendly
points.body: Dada lives on the island of Rügen in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and in daily life she encounters no xenophobia; her neighbours are very friendly to her, her husband, her children and her darker-skinned Nigerian father. But she notices her own fear growing: last weekend her father visited and the two walked around Stralsund, the streets full of AfD campaign posters, the occasional German flag hung in front of an apartment block or a parking lot, and she felt a kind of nausea, wondering ‘whether my father, whether I myself, am seen as not belonging here, as unwelcome’. She says if she saw a French flag in France she wouldn't feel the same unease; but seeing a German flag in the country where she was born, she asks: is this because they love Germany, or because they are far right.

points.h: Germany's last shred of face has been taken too
points.body: Dada says the German model ‘very clearly no longer works’: the economy has long been in stagflation, pillar industries like cars and chemicals have lost competitiveness because of high energy costs, and large numbers of jobs have been cut or moved away. She takes German cars as an example: Germany completely misjudged the relevance of electrification and underestimated Chinese automakers' ability to catch up — it used to be assumed Chinese brands could never have the same prestige as German brands, but now in markets like South Africa, where German cars once sold at a premium, you see BYD and a pile of Chinese brands flooding in, and people no longer care whether it's a BMW or a Mercedes. She says Germany's last remnant of pride — ‘no one in China can build a high-end car brand’ — has now been taken away too.

points.h: America's non-tech sectors are as sick as Germany
points.body: Dada offers a comparison: the US has 150 companies with software revenue over a billion dollars, Europe has only about 30. The Mag 7 together are worth almost half of total global market cap, and economic growth is extremely concentrated in the single sector of tech. But she points out this is not just a European or German problem, it's a technology problem: America's existing non-tech sectors are suffering exactly the same malaise as German and European industry, US economic growth is broadly driven by capex going into data centres, by the tech and AI boom, while non-tech sectors grow at the same rate as mature German and European industry. She stresses, however, that this does not remove a fact: in industries intensive in technology and R&D innovation, Europe simply does not have as strong an industry as the US.

points.h: Europe is absent from every layer of the AI value chain
points.body: Dada breaks the AI value stack into three layers: the chip and infrastructure layer (chips, and the data centres that house them and turn them into training and inference compute); the model layer (the models that actually produce intelligence); and the application layer (using that intelligence to build concrete applications that bring value to people's lives). She says Europe plays too small a role at every layer, and the further down the stack you go, the starker the gap. She argues that without a structural answer to ‘what is American tech, what is Chinese tech’, no amount of transformation effort in Europe will solve this root cause — every other problem compounds and grows out of this root cause.

points.h: 80% of the economy doesn't need the strongest model
points.body: Dada offers a ‘vibes-based number’: of the total value AI creates, 80% does not depend on the strongest Pareto-frontier model; many more efficient, cheaper, possibly open-source models can do the economically valuable work as long as they fall within the intelligence distribution the task requires. Her company is heavily betting on this direction, namely ‘model routing’ — you don't care whether it's model A, B or C, you only care whether at a given moment it's the cheapest, lowest-latency optimal intelligence. The remaining 20% she admits she finds hard to price: that's where frontier intelligence matters, such as drug discovery, adversarial markets like cybersecurity (there's always a better hacker, so you always want the strongest intelligence to attack or defend), hedge funds, critical infrastructure protection. She uses Einstein as an analogy: give a hedge fund a thousand Einsteins and its success rate rises sharply; give Coca-Cola a thousand Einsteins and it won't make it more successful, because that's brand, a century-old formula, distribution and a physical business.

points.h: If you build your own frontier, it has to be a Manhattan Project
points.body: Dada argues that for the 80%, Europe can get by with the existing model landscape, using Chinese models, American models; but for the 20% it is ‘absolutely critical’ — you cannot honestly tell a European that in ten years you can defend their life and secure their access to the modern medicine of that time if you don't secure access to frontier intelligence. There are only two ways to get access: produce it yourself, or trade for access. If you produce it yourself, being third or fourth is not enough, being ‘DeepSeek minus twelve months’ is not enough, it must be a Manhattan-style effort, extremely ambitious, extremely well funded. She admits Europe is already late on the recursive self-improvement loop, but ‘it's not over until it's over’, and even in the last metre of a marathon she will try not to come last. At the same time she says that even if Europe mobilises capital and talent, success is not guaranteed, so it must plan for failure.

points.h: What Europe lacks is not money, it's someone who can make the call
points.body: Dada argues the capital problem is real, but it is not that ‘Europe has no money’ — Europe has pensions, insurers with huge balance sheets, and the European economy is about two-thirds the size of the US. The real problem is a structural absence of the kind of few players the US has: AWS, Google, Microsoft, xAI and OpenAI can coordinate at extremely low cost, xAI can just call OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft. Europe has national borders, different regulations, fragmented capital, far higher coordination costs, and not even a unified financial market. Her solution is not to wait for 27 member states but a ‘coalition of the willing’: the biggest few companies plus the biggest few governments, together pushing pensions and insurance money to allocate more to venture capital. She argues Europe's biggest structural gap is the absence of an Elon Musk figure — someone with enough influence, power and orchestration ability to put all the pieces together, lock people in a room for three days and get the deal done, Manhattan-style.
